Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette: Señor García, a 65-year-old Latin American male with a background in military service and now working as a special education teacher, has been grappling with persistent symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) since his time serving overseas. The traumatic event that continues to haunt him involves an ambush where he tasted the metallic scent of blood mixed with dust—a memory that resurfaces vividly whenever he experiences a similar taste or feels dizzy and lightheaded. Señor García's symptoms began shortly after his deployment, when he first found himself feeling dizzy and lightheaded in crowded classrooms. The dizziness triggered intense flashbacks to the ambush, and he quickly realized that talking about his military experience only exacerbated these sensations. Over time, he adopted various maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming emotional distress. For instance, he would always ensure that he was near an exit whenever he felt any sense of discomfort or was in a crowded space, constantly scanning his environment for signs of threat. His heightened state of hypervigilance and the constant need to identify escape routes became ingrained habits. He believed these strategies were essential for maintaining control over his anxiety. However, they also led to an increased perception of threat; every unexpected or loud sound would send him into a heightened state of alertness, further reinforcing his belief that danger lurked around every corner. The weight of these symptoms had begun to affect Señor García’s work as a special education teacher. His hyperalertness and constant need to check his surroundings for signs of threat made it difficult to fully engage with students. For example, during one particularly noisy classroom activity, he felt overwhelmed by the unexpected sounds, which triggered memories of gunfire. As a result, he became increasingly distant from both his colleagues and students, often finding excuses to leave meetings or avoid group activities. The cycle began to tighten as Señor García’s maladaptive strategies further heightened his perception of threat. His fear that danger was always imminent made him more reliant on staying near exits and checking his surroundings constantly. This hypervigilance in turn led to increased emotional stress, creating a self-reinforcing loop where his coping mechanisms exacerbated the very symptoms they were meant to mitigate. Señor García’s most significant concern was how these symptoms would affect his ability to continue teaching. He feared that if he couldn’t manage his anxiety and maintain control over his environment, he might lose his job—a prospect that filled him with dread. Despite his efforts to cope through avoidance and hypervigilance, the dizziness and taste triggers continued to surface unexpectedly, often in situations where he felt most vulnerable. It was a particularly difficult week at work when Señor García finally decided to seek help. The accumulation of stress from both personal and professional challenges had become overwhelming. He realized that his coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable and began to hope for a way to break the cycle of fear and avoidance without compromising his ability to support his students. In therapy, he expressed a deep desire to regain control over his life and fears, hoping to find strategies that would allow him to continue teaching without the constant threat of his PTSD symptoms. Señor García was determined to address his triggers directly and develop healthier coping mechanisms, with the ultimate goal of reclaiming both his professional role and personal peace of mind.
